q: What is partition pruning?
options: The planner skips partitions that can't contain rows matching the query
explain: It only works when the query filters on the partition key with values the planner (or the executor, for parameters) can compare against partition bounds.

q: A `payments` table is range-partitioned by month. How do you remove data older than 2 years most efficiently?
options: DETACH and DROP the old partitions
explain: Dropping a partition is a metadata operation: instant, no dead rows, no long transaction. A big DELETE creates millions of dead tuples and WAL.

q: In PostgreSQL, what's required for a primary key on a partitioned table?
options: It must include the partition key columns
Partitioned tables can't have primary keys
It must be the partition key alone
explain: Uniqueness is enforced per partition, so global uniqueness is only guaranteed if the partition key is part of the key.

q: An `events` table is partitioned by `created_at`. What happens to `SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 42`?
options: It reads only the newest partition
It fails: the partition key is required
It uses a global index across partitions
explain: With no condition on created_at, nothing can be pruned. PostgreSQL has no global indexes, so each partition's index on user_id is searched.

q: What's the main risk of asynchronous replication?
options: On failover, transactions committed on the leader but not yet replicated are lost; replicas can serve stale data
Replicas can't be used for reads
The leader can't accept writes when a replica is down
explain: The commit returns before replicas confirm. That's the price of low latency; synchronous replication avoids the loss but slows every commit.

q: A user updates their profile, refreshes the page, and sees the old data. Reads go to a replica. What's this?
explain: Fixes: read the user's own data from the leader for a short time after a write, route the session to one node, or wait for the replica to catch up to the write's position.

q: What do read replicas scale?
explain: Every replica still applies every write. Scaling writes means sharding (or batching, or a bigger leader).

q: How does sharding differ from partitioning?
options: Sharding spreads data across separate database servers; partitioning splits a table within one database
Partitioning is across servers; sharding is within one
Sharding is only for NoSQL databases
explain: The terms get mixed (Cassandra and Kafka call their shards partitions), but in relational interviews this is the usual distinction.

q: Orders are range-sharded by `created_at`. What's the problem?
options: All new writes go to the last shard: a hot shard
explain: A monotonically increasing key concentrates the write load. Hashing the key, or sharding by tenant/user, spreads it.

q: What's the main downside of hash-based sharding?
options: Range queries on the key must hit all shards
explain: Hashing destroys ordering. Point lookups by key are fast; "all orders from last week" becomes scatter-gather.

q: What's the advantage of consistent hashing?
options: Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys
It guarantees perfectly even load without virtual nodes
It removes the need for replication
explain: Each node owns arcs of a hash ring. A new node takes over parts of its neighbors' arcs; everything else stays where it was.

q: Why is `shard = hash(key) % N` a problem when you add a shard?
options: Changing N remaps almost every key to a different shard
The modulo operation is too slow
It only works for numeric keys
explain: Going from 4 to 5 shards moves about 80% of keys. Consistent hashing, or a fixed large number of logical shards mapped to physical nodes, avoids it.

q: One celebrity account gets 1000× more traffic than others and overloads its shard. What helps?
options: Splitting the hot key (e.g. adding a suffix to spread it) and caching its reads
explain: More shards don't help a single key. Write splitting (key#1..key#10, merged on read) and aggressive caching do.

q: How do you avoid cross-shard joins between customers and their orders?
options: Shard both by customer_id so a customer's data lives on one shard
Join in the application with N queries
explain: Co-location by a shared shard key keeps the common queries single-shard. Citus calls these co-located distributed tables.

q: How do you generate unique IDs across many shards?
options: Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp + node + sequence) or UUIDv7
explain: Per-shard sequences collide. Snowflake IDs are 64-bit, roughly time-ordered and generated without coordination.

q: According to CAP, what must a distributed database choose during a network partition?
options: Nothing: modern databases avoid the trade-off
explain: Partitions happen, so P isn't optional. A CP system refuses some requests; an AP system answers with possibly stale data.

q: In a leaderless store with N=3 replicas, which setting guarantees that reads see the latest acknowledged write?
explain: W + R > N means every read quorum overlaps every write quorum. In practice edge cases (sloppy quorums, concurrent writes) still weaken this.

q: What is vertical partitioning?
options: Splitting tables or columns into separate tables or databases, e.g. by domain
Adding more CPU to the server
explain: Moving rarely used wide columns to a side table, or each microservice owning its own database, are both vertical splits.

q: A PostgreSQL database is getting slow under load. What should you try before sharding?
options: Indexes and query fixes, caching, read replicas, partitioning, a bigger machine
Sharding is always the first step
explain: Sharding adds permanent complexity. A single modern server handles a lot; many companies run very large PostgreSQL instances before needing shards.

q: What is Citus?
options: A PostgreSQL extension that distributes tables across nodes (sharding)
explain: Citus shards tables by a distribution column and routes or parallelizes queries. Vitess is the equivalent for MySQL (born at YouTube).

q: Physical vs logical replication in PostgreSQL?
options: Physical streams WAL for the whole cluster (exact copy); logical replicates row changes for selected tables
Physical replicates SQL statements; logical replicates files
They're two names for the same thing
explain: Physical replicas are read-only clones of the same major version. Logical replication works across versions (useful for upgrades) and lets you pick tables.

q: What's the cost of synchronous replication?
options: Higher commit latency, and writes stall if the synchronous replica is unavailable
It doubles storage on the leader
explain: Each commit waits for the replica's confirmation. Setups usually list several candidates (`ANY 1 (r1, r2)`) so one replica outage doesn't stop writes.

q: PACELC extends CAP. What does the "ELC" part say?
options: Else (no partition), choose between latency and consistency
explain: Even without failures, waiting for replicas to agree costs latency. DynamoDB-style systems choose latency; Spanner-style choose consistency.
